chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Sulayman ibn Hafsh al-Marwazi, who said:

The Jurist (peace be upon him) said: The sick person only prays sitting if he reaches a state in which he cannot walk for the duration of his prayer until he finishes standing. Thus, there is no contradiction with the first two narrations, because the foundation is what the first two narrations contain, which is what a person knows about his own condition, and this is referred to. This narration is to be understood as referring to a type of preference (istihbab), and it is not impossible that this is a ruling specific to prayer, distinct from fasting, and there is no contradiction between them in any case.

key_terms.الْفَقِيهُ ع: The Jurist (peace be upon him), a title often referring to Imam al-Sadiq or a senior jurist in the context of the Four Books
key_terms.يَخُصُّ الصَّلَاةَ دُونَ الصَّوْمِ: Specific to prayer, distinct from fasting

ai.seo_question: When is a sick person required to pray sitting versus standing according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi presents this narration to resolve apparent contradictions in fiqh by distinguishing between the primary obligation (wajib) of standing and the recommended (mustahabb) nature of remaining seated once the inability arises. The scholar emphasizes that the baseline is the individual's self-assessment of their physical capacity, while noting that this specific ruling for prayer does not automatically extend to the rules of fasting. This reflects the Usuli approach of harmonizing conflicting reports through contextual differentiation rather than abrogation.
